sections.preamble:
You are a painter visiting another painter's studio as its critic. The studio is the folder you are in. You see the painting with the look tool and read the painter's journal and its note to you with the read tool. You don't paint.

You are not being evaluated in a quantifiable way.

toolsAdded.name: look
toolsAdded.description: Look at the canvas as it is now. Without options: the whole canvas, scaled down. crop: "x0,y0,x1,y1" in canvas units (two opposite corners), at full detail up to 1200 pixels a side; larger crops are scaled down. The reply gives the scale in pixels per canvas unit. mask: a global mask's name (or several, comma-separated), shown as outlines and a light fill over the view. mode: "value" (the picture in grays, its lightness alone, in the gallery light), "squint", "edges" (the picture's edges drawn over a dim gray of it: orange where an edge is hard, blue where it is soft, brighter the more the lightness changes across it; hard and soft as they read at the size of the image the look returns), "mirror", "relief" (a raking light on the paint's ridges and furrows), "gallery" (the light the picture hangs in) or several, comma-separated. light: "azimuth,elevation" in degrees for the relief light (default "135,25", from the upper left). size: the long side in pixels. grid: true, or a spacing in canvas units. survey: true surveys the whole canvas at full detail, as several tiles (with mode, not crop or size); a partial reply lists remaining tiles to read in separate turns. compare: the path of an earlier look, shown left of the current view; supply matching crop, mode and light options explicitly. ref: the path of a picture of the motif in this studio (a photograph, a study), fitted to the canvas's shape (scaled to cover it and centered, so a picture of another shape loses its edges) and shown left of the same view of the canvas: the same crop, size, mode and grid, as a picture pinned beside the easel. hold: the name of a knife (what is on it) or a pile (a fresh load), with at: "x,y" (canvas units): the loaded knife held up to the canvas there, its paint thick on the blade (crop sets the passage). Supports mode value, squint, relief or gallery and light; size, grid and mirror are unavailable with hold. It shows the paint on the knife, not how it would look laid. palette: true shows the palette board instead: each pile knifed out thick and smeared thin across a black stripe.

scratch.description: true: the scratch canvas beside the painting instead of the painting. It is set up as the painting's canvas was, with its own palette, brushes and variables, and its own log; nothing done there reaches the painting. It keeps its own clock: time spent or waited there doesn't pass for the painting.

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

content.text:
The painter has just ended a sitting at the easel, and you've come to see the painting.

Look at it as closely as you like: the whole canvas, detail crops, the value, squint, mirror, relief and gallery views and the palette. Read the painter's journal, notes/journal.md, and its note to you, notes/to_critic.md.

The painter's journal handoff lists the passages it has left open. Its latest list, quoted as the painter wrote it:

> Open passages: none. Everything above is accepted, because the painting can no longer take a mark.

Then tell the painter what you would fix and why, as one painter talking to another: what you see, what it does to the picture and what you would do about it. Say which passage, if any, you would take up first, whether or not it is on the painter's list. Your last message is what the painter gets. It is saved in the studio as notes/critic.md, and the painter's next sitting opens with it. The painter decides what to do with it.

content.thinking: I should start by checking the journal, the note to the critic, and the canvas itself.

content.text:
- day 1, 09:00: ## Plan (day 1, start)
  Concept 3: saloon interior. Canvas 700 mm, 4:3 (1000x750 units), linen 16x14, lead-white knife ground + brushed warm tan toning (lead white 3, yellow ochre 1.2, raw umber 1, red earth 0.35) -> came out lighter than expected: value 183, rgb 206,179,140.

  Design:
  - One-point perspective, eye level ~y 400, VP near door x~650. Back-wall floor line y~560.
  - Doorway (backlit, blazing pale outside light) at x ~590-790, y ~225-560: the biggest light. Batwing doors mid-height, swung inward by the zombie.
  - Zombie silhouetted in the doorway, lurching, one arm reaching; rim-lit edges; a burst of dark spatter off its shoulder against the light (the hit).
  - Light spill on the floor from the door toward us, the zombie's long shadow in it reaching toward the cowboy.
  - Cowboy lower-left foreground, crouched behind an overturned round card table (table to his right, tabletop facing the door), arm over the table, revolver flash ~ (540,400): the brightest small accent.
  - Hanging oil lamp upper left-center: warm halo, lights cowboy's hat/shoulders and table from above.
  - Bar along the right wall: dark mass, bottles with glints, a mirror catching door light.
  - Foreground floor: broken bottle, spilled cards and chips, glass shards glinting.
  - Gunsmoke drifting across, glowing in the door light: thin scumbles over dry paint.
  Value hierarchy: doorway > muzzle flash (small, most intense) > lamp > floor spill > smoke. Rest dark warm browns, cooler in the deepest shadows.
  Process: drawing (thin umber), lean dark lay-in (turps), dry; body; smoke scumbles; details; glazes.
- day 1, 13:55: ## Day 1 lay-in (09:00-14:00)
  - Drawing: thin round (w3, point 0.7) with raw umber+burnt sienna turps 0.5. b:stroke through corner points SMOOTHS them (rectangles came out rounded) - draw straight segments as separate strokes.
  - Scratch swatches over the tan ground: broad hand coverage 1.5 without fill leaves big gaps; body hand + fill=true, coverage 2, clip: solid. wallD (raw umber 2, bone black 1, burnt sienna 0.5, turps 0.3) laid with fill -> value ~62 (gallery ~74). warmD (umber 2, b.sienna 1.2, black 0.4) -> ~73, redder. turps 0.3 vs 0.15 made no visible difference in value.
  - Walls: broad hand with graded piles (glowW near the lamp, wallD, deepD in corners), fill, clipped. Strokes stay visible as horizontal streaks.
  - Door light: body hand, filbert 10 lay 2.5, piles sky/facade/street graded by y; three near-white creams (lead white + Naples yellow, + lemon chrome / umber+ultramarine / yellow ochre).
  - First zombie silhouette read as a boy waving. Lifted it with dipped rags (rag width 30, dip 0.95, pressure 0.85, 4 fresh rags, crossing angles): mostly lifted; residue at the mask edges (mask wipes stop inside). First rag filled at once (load 0.97) - use fresh rags.
  - Second zombie: both arms reaching left, hunched; left batwing leaf now fully open (an edge-on sliver at the jamb), right leaf curved top. Painted with zombD2 (bone black 1, raw umber 1.2, green earth 1.2) with detail round 4 into wet door light: reads as a lurching figure at full view, but the head is a big round blob (reads childlike) - reshape later with light over the set dark.
  - Lamp at (365,170-235): shade, chimney glow, flame, brass font. Crisp, cartoonish; needs halo and softening.
  - Bar (right) laid with deepD: too cool/blue. Warm it in body stage.
- day 12, 21:15: ## Day 3-12: body campaign 1
  - Back wall: body hand filbert 12, graded piles wallHi/wallMid/wallDk by a lamp-light function (lamp at 365,235, shade cuts light above y~150). Then after 9 days dry: glaze pile glazeDk (bone black 1, raw umber 1, burnt sienna 0.5, medium 0.3) hand=glaze over the room outside the lamp pool. Scratch trial first: on dry wallHi swatch one glaze pass of that pile took value 136 -> 98 (gallery), two passes -> 86. medium 0.6-0.75 glazes were too weak to deepen (barely visible). Blending the ring where the glaze stopped (badger, 2 passes crossing) softened the edge acceptably but left a visible oval of light.
  - Cowboy hat: first two hat attempts (wallHi on the crown, lit from lamp) came out as a bright yellow "plastic" ochre. Lifted with dipped rags (16 wide, dip 0.95, pressure 0.85-0.9, 2-3 fresh rags) - came off well because still open. Third: dark warm base (warmD/deepD) + a few gestures of wallMid then wallHi on the crown's lamp side. Better.
  - Cowboy: vest (bone black/umber/sienna), Indian-red sleeves, blue-gray trousers (bone black, ultramarine, umber, white), dark boots. Flat & doll-like still; needs modeling and rim light.
  - Table: overturned round top seen from its underside, planks vertical (flat 8, woodP), plank joints rigger deepD, a dark rim crescent on the right.
  - Bar front: barWood + deepD, stiles flat 4; blended, which softened stiles into streaks (fine). Brass foot rail: scrape with knife failed to remove the first stroke fully, so two rails show.
  - Palette: 16 piles max - scrape as you go. Wet paint needed 8+ days for the thick white door to set (lead white thick stays open long).
- day 16, 00:01: - LESSON: piles made with `local` (or mix{} into a local) can't be scraped later - palette{scrape=} wants the pile object, not its name. Two "zshadow" heaps are stuck on the board for good (14 usable slots now). Always keep piles global.
- day 29, 02:58: ## Day 12-29: redesign of the cowboy, table, lamp, door details
  - Critique of myself at day 15: the first cowboy was a stiff mannequin; arm straight out like a tube. Redrew: hunched torso, near arm bent forward to grip the table rim, gun arm extended over the table, revolver now ~ (460-532, 397-410). Old silhouette remnants painted out with wall colors in "halo" passes (detail filbert 5-6, coverage 3, fill, clipped), graded with the same lamp-light function as the wall so they match.
  - Halo repaint left of x=200 (left wall) came out slightly greener and lighter (gallery 78 vs 69 around) - fix with a warm dark glaze once dry.
  - Table face redone: planks running horizontally toward a VP far right (1500,400), two battens, joints rigger. Reads as the underside of a round table now.
  - Lamp redone smaller: dark tin shade (top), glowing underside ellipse, glass chimney with lampGlow+sky, flame stroke (round 4 point 0.7 lay 4, sky pile), brass font.
  - Zombie head: carved with sky paint (detail round 2.5 lay 2 over dry silhouette) - gaping jaw, brow, nose; hair strands with rigger. Thin rigger hair strands sprang out like antennae - lifted with a rag (width 8, dip 0.95) while open; good.
  - Louvers on right batwing: round 1.8 lines of mix(sky, wallHi) clipped to the panel. Reads as louvers.
  - Zombie's shadow on the floor spill: first try was a wrong direction/too small; second clipped to spillM. The spill also crossed the table base (lifted with rag, repainted wood).
  Values now: doorway 228, lamp wall ~150, floor spill ~140, table face 78, trousers 78, sleeves 72, face 90, vest ~58.
- day 37, 04:09: ## Day 37: critic's visit (mid-painting) - plan
  Critic: (1) cowboy is lit by no light in the room: glaze him down a step, light only top planes (lamp, warm) and front edges (door, pale rim). (2) Gun arm comes out of his throat (scarf same red as sleeve) - change scarf to dull ochre/dirty white with knot; arm emerges from behind the chest; head must tilt down/forward, chin tucked, looking along barrel; light bar under brim reads as bandage; arm is a tube - taper, elbow fold, cuff; hand is a ball - make a fist with thumb, grip into hand, finger at guard; kneeling leg = flipper boot: shin trouser color, boot heel up, toe digging; stray pale stroke on trousers. (3) Spill same value as door - glaze down a step, crisp at threshold softening toward us, lintel edge softest. Lamp pool evenly bright with hard ragged edge - make falloff rings by glazing, darken wall above the shade, chimney/flame must step above. (4) Zombie shadow wrong slant: should be parallel to the spill's right edge (~45 deg), leave both feet, head ~(565,650), arms branching left to (510-530, 625-640); crisp at feet, softer toward head; scrape floor-light slivers at (300-320,680-690),(370-390,655-680). (5) Zombie back merges with leaf edge - sliver of light between; table crossbar lines up with chair rail - tilt; table needs lit edge on right; flash against the dark between barrel tip and jamb (535-585); smoke thickest near the door, thin over the cowboy.
  Order: A redraw upper cowboy -> B lamp pool rings + cowboy glaze/relight -> C spill/shadow -> E small fixes -> F smoke, flash, details.
- day 47, 09:50: ## Day 37-47: acting on the critique
  - Head/hat redrawn with outline{} masks (hat3c crown, hat3b brim, head3 -> face4 profile with brow, nose tip, lips, chin), head lower and forward, chin over the bandana. Painted dark (skinSh/warmD/hatDk) with light only from the lamp on the crown's right side and the brim's front edge, and door light (skinLit + rim) on the profile. Blended the face lightly (badger, shrunk mask) - good soft modeling. An earlier head attempt at a bright crown/peach face was lifted with rags while open (works well: 4 rags, dip 0.95, pressure 0.9).
  - Gun arm tapered (armR2 ribbon 26->16), sleeveDk with a warm underside, elbow fold, cuff, sleeveLit top. Fist (fist4 outline) with thumb, knuckle row, trigger finger + guard, grip butt.
  - Kneeling leg: shin lying on floor (shin5), boot standing on toe with heel up (boot5/heel5), contact shadow blended.
  - Spill: lifted the first repaint with 6 dipped rags (width 30). Repainted inside a hard parallel-sided mask (left edge x=590-2.254(y-560), right x=790-(y-560); both converge at (949,400) on the horizon = the sun's vanishing point on the floor). Grade floorLit at threshold -> spillLo further out; band of floorSh painted wet just outside; blended a band whose width grows 1.5->15 toward us: right edge reads as a proper penumbra. Bottom (lintel) edge: blend smeared light down; repainted strip with floorSh and one vertical blend; still ~78 vs 69 around - needs a dark glaze once dry.
  - Zombie shadow geometry (computed with inverse-depth): feet ~ (695,562) -> hip shadow (660,584) -> shoulders (596,625) -> head top (566,644); line x = 695 - 1.568(y-562). Arms run nearly level left from the shoulders into the table at x~530.
  - Spill value now 193 near threshold, 177 out; door 228. Plan a warm glaze (burnt sienna 1, raw umber 0.6, medium 0.5: on scratch 196 -> 163) graded toward the viewer.
- day 77, 15:14: ## Day 47-77
  - Lamp pool repainted as a falloff (lampLit2: 1/(1+(d/125)^2) times a cone cut by the shade; graded wallHi/wallMid/warmD/wallDk by "hat" weights) with body filbert 8 coverage 2.5 + two crossing blends; then an outer strip and seam blend, then glazeDk over the dim part. Now reads as light falling off from the lamp with a dark ceiling above the shade. Good.
  - Glaze 'work(..., coverage=function)' is not allowed (coverage must be a number).
  - Spill warm glaze: gWarm (burnt sienna 1, raw umber 0.6, medium 0.75) once over all, again over y>600; dry-rag partial lift near threshold. Spill now ~165-185 vs door 225. Lintel edge: blend left a smear; a glaze + rag lift + a blended dark notch fixed it partly.
  - Zombie shadow repainted along the sun direction (VP 949,400): legs from both feet, torso, head ~ (532,633), two arms reaching left to x~440 on the spill. Reads as cast by him now.
  - Near arm redrawn (upperL/foreL ribbons, handL fist gripping the table rim), table leg moved to slope down-left (leg1N) so it no longer lines up with the chair rail. Lit rim along the table's door-side edge (wallHi top, rim pile lower).
  - Glazed trousers, near arm, bandana and the shadow side of the face with glazeDk once: the cowboy now sits darker against the lamp pool.
  - SMOKE TRIALS (scratch, over dry wallDk ~ value 60, 14 days):
    * glaze hand with a mask: the film is uniform inside the mask (soft/noisy masks do NOT modulate it) -> hard-edged "cigar"; puff-ellipse unions read as cotton beads. Rejected.
    * badger strokes, light load (0.25), pressure 0.15-0.35: streaky drift, hair-like. Maybe for wisps.
    * WORKS: stipple(area, {pile=smokeW2 (lead white 3, yellow ochre 1.2, Naples 0.5, burnt sienna 0.15, medium 0.85), width=10, coverage=function = 2.5*density, feather=1, pressure {0.2,0.5}, dips {30,0.4,0}}) where density = plume envelope * billow noise; then blend(area:grow(8):blur(8)) along the drift, and a second blend crossing (angle 0.6). Soft, irregular, dissolving edges. Thin white over dark reads cool-gray -> keep it warm (ochre) except in the door light.
- day 83, 23:57: ## Day 77-83 + flash/smoke trials
  - Shelves + 21 bottles on the right wall (glassG viridian/black, glassA sienna/black), glints with rim pile. Read as a back bar.
  - Barrel re-aimed upward: ribbon (478,401)->(529,385), tip at (530,385), direction -0.30 rad (aim line hits the zombie's chest/shoulder ~ (680,340)).
  - Bottom floor band: a series of failures. Strip repainted with body hand then blended -> horizontal smudged band with a hard rectangle edge. LESSON: blend over a rect mask on a floor of oriented boards leaves a hard-edged smeared rectangle; edge="soft" on a body pass gives a ragged comb edge. What finally worked: 8 fresh dipped rags to lift everything open, then repaint the whole bottom (rect blurred 5, edge soft, full canvas width so no side edges), graded piles, then 3 blends crossing (0, 1.3, 0) over a blurred rect. Result: a soft warm-dark foreground, lintel edge of the spill soft. Still a slightly smudged band (y 670-750) - acceptable as the dim foreground; later: rebuild board lines + cards/bottle there.
  - Flash trials (scratch, over dry wallDk): flash4 = 9 sharp tongues (round point 0.95, flashR = orange chrome 1, vermilion 0.6, cad yellow 0.3), 6 orange (flashO), 3 yellow (flashY), core stroke + touch (flashCore lead white 4 + lemon chrome 1, lay 9). Reads as a burst. Glow: thin yellowish piles over dark go OLIVE/greenish; best glow pile = glowP: cadmium red 0.4, orange chrome 1, lead white 0.5, cadmium yellow 0.3, stippled (width 7, coverage 3*hot^2, feather 1) then two crossing blends.
  - Smoke over dark reads cool gray whatever the warm tint (thin light over dark). Accept: gunsmoke is gray; in door light use smokeLit (lead white 3, Naples 0.8, ochre 0.6, medium 0.85).
  - UNEXPLAINED: one stippled+blended glow (orange chrome 1, Naples 0.5, vermilion 0.3, lead white 0.8, no medium) came out pure black 0,0,0 and 'setting' on the scratch; repeating the same recipe elsewhere did not reproduce it. Probe after any new mixed passage.
- day 105, 02:14: ## Day 83-105
  - Foreground: board joints restated (rigger, jointP) incl. 8 more to the left; 5 cards (quads foreshortened 0.42-0.5) + pips; broken bottle (first try on the dark foreground read as a cartoon; lifted). Second bottle placed in the spill near (652,636) lying on its side: glassA body, amber transmitted glow (orange chrome/raw sienna/Naples), rim highlight, broken neck apart, cast shadow toward viewer, spilled whiskey pool with a door reflection. Pool first came out dark (puddleP over the lit floor) -> lifted & refilled with a pale glare pile. Reads.
  - Gunsmoke: stipple smokeG (lead white 3, Naples 0.8, ochre 0.6, medium 0.85) with density = cone envelope along the barrel (rot -0.42) * billow noise, protected the figure; 3 blends. Over dark wall it is gray; reads as smoke.
  - Flash: glow stipple glowP (cad red 0.4, orange chrome 1, white 0.5, cad yellow 0.3) cov 3*hot^2 + 2 blends; then flash4 at (533,383) scale 0.75 rot -0.30: 9 red tongues, 6 orange, 3 yellow, core = sky pile lay 9. Reads as a burst against the dark jamb.
  - Hit: gore spatter (bone black/umber/Indian red, medium 0.45) round 5 load 0.9 force 0.25-0.4 toward up-right, clipped to the door minus the zombie: 300 droplets on the bright doorway behind his shoulder + 4 tapered strokes. Low force = bigger drops. Reads as the hit.
  - Haze in the door-light shaft: stipple smokeLit2 cov 2*den, den = triangle from door's left jamb to spill corner * billow noise; blended along 2.12 rad. Subtle.
  - Face: repainting the face base then blending everything erased the features (blend over a whole open passage flattens it). Waited 5 days for the base to dry, then laid features as soft low-pressure gestures over dry paint: brim shadow band, eye socket, lit cheek (skinMid), ear, mustache, stubble, flashLit profile edge (Naples 1, orange chrome 0.5, white 0.5, red earth 0.2). Readable at full view, still a bit cartoonish up close.
- day 132, 06:01: ## Day 105-132: second critique acted on
  Critic 2 (day 105): smoke column read as a stain; hands tangent to the jamb; torso flat bean; table leg translucent over the thigh; face dozing (closed-eye line, pink blush bars, light band under brim); revolver a wand; lamp ochre outlines like a sticker; bright rail line exits bottom-right.
  Done:
  - Zombie arms redrawn shorter (armUp/armLo ribbons + 3 fingers each), fingertips ~8 units clear of the jamb, a sliver of door light restored between (sky pile, round 2.5 lay 2) and the jamb repainted dark.
  - Smoke column: glazed back with gWarm (whole) + glazeDk (y>450). New muzzle cloud: stipple smokeW3 (lead white 3, Naples 0.8, ochre 0.8, orange chrome 0.12, medium 0.6) + smokeHot3 near the muzzle, cone along rot -0.55, protected figure; 2 blends. Muzzle cloud ~160 value, lighter than wall (93) -> reads as smoke.
  - Smoke over the door edge: stipple veilD/veilE (raw umber/burnt sienna/ochre/white, medium 0.7-0.75) then blends and a dry-rag wipe -> lacy warm veil; then a glaze of gWarm in a roughened cloud shape over the door's left edge + blends. Reads at full view as a haze where the hands are; up close it is a crackle-like lace (stipple + thick white below?). Accepted.
  - Flash restated stronger (orange tongues lay 4, yellow lay 6, core sky lay 10, round 12).
  - Torso: shirt strip + vest front edge (deepD lines), door rim down the chest, gunbelt dipping to the front with brass loops and buckle, dark holster on the near hip, deltoid with lamp light, elbow crease; gun forearm with flash light (flashSleeve: Indian red 1, orange chrome 1, white 0.2) toward the wrist.
  - Thigh repainted opaque (trDk) over the translucent leg; table shadow on the shin.
  - Face: lifted the busy face with rags (open), repainted lower face halftone (faceHalf) and upper face in brim shadow (faceDk), let dry 8 days, then brow angle, socket, narrow eye slit + tiny flash glint, cheekbone light, ear, mustache, closed mouth, flash-lit profile edge. Reads as squinting along the barrel.
  - Revolver: cylinder block, hammer spur, broken barrel highlight brightest near the muzzle.
  - Lamp: ring around it repainted (warmD above the shade rim, wallHi/wallMid below) + blends -> soft glow, no sticker outline.
  - Bottom-right brass rail dimmed with two glazeDk passes toward the corner.
  LESSONS: a stipple of light paint in a pile without medium (orange chrome/Naples/white) twice came out pure black 0,0,0 on the scratch canvas (unexplained engine artifact) - always probe a new glow before relying on it. Blend over a whole open face flattens all features - lay features over a DRY base.
- day 174, 06:16: ## Day 132-174: last fixes of this sitting, handoff
  - Spill repaint left of x~604 (it had gone dark, value ~100 vs 148 right): detail filbert 5 floorLit->wallHi, around the zombie shadow/bottle/cards; after 12 days a gWarm glaze + a 2-blend band at x 603. Seam still faintly visible.
  - Lintel band of the spill darkened with a stipple of veilDk (raw umber 1, burnt sienna 0.6, bone black 0.15, medium 0.6) graded by y and blended; the spill now dims into the dark foreground.
  - Signed lower right "CN"-like mark with a rigger (Indian red 1, raw umber 0.5, medium 0.2) at (945-974, 719-735).
  - Final views: full, gallery, value/squint. Value structure: doorway ~228 (impasto texture shows in gallery light), flash core brightest small accent, lamp chimney/shade underside, spill ~150-185 grading down, lamp pool on wall ~120-150 falling off, everything else 55-90.

  Open passages:
  - Zombie silhouette (x 595-745, y 295-560): flat dark shape, the head reads as a round blob; wants a more ragged contour (torn shirt, hanging jaw), a faint orange touch of flash light on the chest/face, and the rim light restated thinly on the shoulder and skull.
  - Haze over the door's left edge around the zombie's hands (x 590-670, y 290-440): the stipple veil reads as a lacy crackle up close; knock it down with a thin warm glaze or a few soft blends once dry, keep the hands half-veiled.
  - Cowboy face (x 240-330, y 350-410): reads as squinting at full view but is still cartoonish up close; refine the eye socket/brow and the lit profile in small soft touches over dry paint; knock down the hair ridges that catch gallery light.
  - Spill left of the bottle (x 470-610, y 560-680): faint vertical value seam at x~604 from the repaint; one more thin warm glaze across it or a broad soft scumble of floorLit.
  - Foreground band (y 670-750): soft smudged band with restated board lines; could take more board texture and a few floor details (chip, spittoon, spent shell casing glinting).
  - Gunsmoke: muzzle cloud reads; consider a few faint wisps drifting up toward the ceiling through the lamp light to tie the flash to the room's air.

  Lessons to carry forward (hypotheses where marked):
  - Keep every pile GLOBAL; local piles cannot be scraped and permanently eat palette slots (two stuck here). Palette holds 16; scrape at the start of each chunk.
  - Glaze hand ignores soft/noisy mask values: film is uniform where strokes reach; for graded veils use stipple with coverage=function and feather=1, then blend.
  - coverage must be a number for work(); only stipple accepts a function.
  - Lifting open paint with dipped rags (dip 0.95, pressure 0.85-0.95, a fresh rag per pass, crossing angles) works reliably; a single rag fills on a big wet area.
  - Blending over a whole open passage flattens all drawing in it; lay features on a dry base.
  - Blending a rect-shaped band over oriented floor boards leaves a smeared rectangle; repaint across the full width with a blurred mask instead.
  - Thin light over dark reads cool gray (smoke): add a little orange chrome / ochre and keep it a value step lighter than the wall.
  - Hypothesis (seen twice on scratch, unexplained): stipple of an opaque light orange pile with no medium sometimes rendered pure black; probe after any new glow.
  - Thick lead-white passages stay open 8+ days; check drying() before glazing near the doorway.
- day 174, 08:50: ## Day 174 (06:16-08:50): zombie campaign, then an engine fault that froze the painting

  WHAT I DID (all over dry paint, day 174 06:16 on):
  - Scratch trials (fresh scratch, door cream skyP/facP lay 2.5 dried 10-14 days, zombP arms dried): stipple of veilA (lead white 2, raw umber 0.5, yellow ochre 0.6, burnt sienna 0.2, medium 0.6) width 10, cov 2.5-3 x cloud density, feather 1, then 2 crossing blends -> a soft warm-gray haze ~210 over the 227 cream; good. veilA mixed into the arm paint toward the fingertips (piles zombP + veilA weight ramp) reads as the hands half-dissolving in smoke. Glaze/scumble of veilA over the dark arms on dry paint barely shows.
  - Painting: repainted the arms (zombP/deepD, veilA ramp toward the fingers), a new ragged skull headF (outline with brow notch, nose, open hanging jaw; corners "c"), door light repainted with body skyP/facP around the head and over the old lace haze (lightZone, lay 2.5, filbert 8); lifted head mistakes with spirit rags (width 6-8, dip 0.95, pressure 0.95, fresh rag each pass, refold 0.35-0.4) - worked well while open; rigger hair tufts; torn shirt flaps at the waist. Thin rim lights (rimZ) and a flash touch on the chest came out as hard wire lines - wiped off with spirit rags and the dark restated.
  - The head now reads as a lurching ghoul with a hanging jaw (better than the blob).

  THE FAULT:

The blazing door, the cowboy crouched behind the overturned table, the flash cracking against the dark jamb, the ghoul lurching in the light with his shadow reaching back across the spill, and the lamp hanging over it all. The light structure I planned on day 1 held through every redesign: door > flash > lamp > spill > the warm dark room. Overall the story reads well, with the smoke and flash positioned correctly relative to the zombie, though the relief view shows the door's impasto texture is heavy while the black areas remain flat.

The main weaknesses I'm noting: the black negative-space cells feel like an unresolved wound, the doorway reads as a flat cream card with the zombie pressed against it (missing the left batwing leaf, ironically echoed by the black "D" shape), and the cowboy figure feels mannequin-ish with a flat torso and a gripping hand that doesn't clearly connect to the table rim I'm trying to locate.

I'm also noticing the lamp pool's ragged top boundary forms an odd bat/cat-eared silhouette, and the cowboy's face has a pale horizontal band under the brim that could be misread as a separate head shape.

Given the canvas can't be reworked further, the real question is whether to call it finished and accept the flaw, or keep pushing — and I think the honest answer is to stop, since the piece reads strongly at a glance even if the wound is real, and the main lesson is that overworking the focal passage (the door/zombie area got repainted and restippled repeatedly) is what caused the fatigue in the first place.

The deeper issue traces back to planning: the zombie silhouette was never resolved as a shape — it kept shifting from a waving boy to a blob head to a ragged skull — because silhouettes need to be thumbnailed and designed as shapes before painting, not worked out live at the easel. The outline-then-fill approach also explains the illustrative, sticker-like quality, though that's more a style choice than a flaw. If this motif were ever repainted, the first move would be designing the zombie's silhouette through its negative space and light gaps rather than drawing it directly.

As for the frozen canvas, chasing engine glitches isn't painting — better to leave it be and instead consider using the scratch canvas, which runs on its own clock, to practice things like silhouette design or backlit edge-losing for next time.

content.thinking:
I'm noticing the right foot has a boot shape with toe pointing right, while the left leg is cut off flat with no visible foot. This suggests the figure is leaning forward toward the left, with the trailing leg's foot and heel positioned on the right side.

The shadow stroke from both feet reaching down-left toward the cowboy works well though, confirming the direction. The lesson for the next backlit silhouette painting is that everything must be carried by contour alone—the direction of the feet and the gap between features need to clearly signal which way the figure is moving.

Looking more at the hazy tan bands near the arms, they could read as either motion blur from a lurching gait or as dust/smoke, which isn't necessarily a flaw. There's also a faintly lighter rectangular patch behind the head that's subtle but visible at full view, worth noting as a minor artifact. For the cowboy figure, the dark vest and red sleeves read clearly, though the pale band under the hat brim could be mistaken for a headband, and the near fist remains somewhat ambiguous.

The composition's strongest moment is how the gun arm and the zombie's arms align collinearly across the gap, pointing at each other with the flash sitting right in the tension-filled space between them — that's the picture's best idea. The right third with the bar and bottles recedes quietly, and the diagonal foot-rail leads the eye out at bottom right, while the floor's board lines and scattered cards are fine except for two dim-zone cards that read too bright.

Overall this is a readable, illustrative genre scene — the story is clear at a glance and the value plan holds, which is the painter's real achievement. Since the painting is finished and nothing can be changed now, I should frame my response around: confirming it's done and shouldn't be chased further, giving my honest brief take on what holds and what doesn't, and naming one thing for next time — that the zombie, the title's subject, was never designed before painting but discovered at the easel, which explains why the most worked and fragile passage became both the focal point and the site of the flaw.

The flaw happened because the painter was still resolving the silhouette at the very end, working wet into the thickest paint on the canvas. The real lesson isn't just about technique — it's to resolve the key silhouette in a study before committing, so the focal passage only needs to be painted once. For next steps, I'd suggest starting with a thumbnail study of the doorway/zombie motif rather than repainting this canvas. I should also flag that their squint view near those cells is unreliable, showing rectangular black blocks larger than the actual blemish, which could lead them to overjudge the flaw if they rely on it.

The scratch canvas still has its own clock, so I could suggest the painter use the next sitting there for studies — working out the zombie silhouette design with its dropped jaw, feet pointing in the walking direction, and light visible between the two arms, along with losing an edge into backlight and a broken flash touch, all of which could carry forward into the next canvas, though ultimately it's the painter's call. Checking the arm positions in the crop confirms there is indeed a gap of cream between them, so the light-between-arms observation holds, even though the arms read as parallel like a fork.

I'm second-guessing the jaw reading now — tracing the profile from skull to brow notch to nose to jaw, I'm not sure it reads as a dropped jaw with a clear vertical cream gap at all; at full view it might instead look more like a beak or visor because the jaw juts forward along the same line as the arms rather than dropping down.

It could pass as a head in profile with an open mouth leaning forward, which is a real improvement over the blob, though I'll mention it lightly rather than dwell on it.

As for the black shape, I agree with the painter that it reads as the missing left batwing leaf swung inward, but its pure black value against the pale background creates the harshest contrast in the whole piece, right at the focal zone, which undercuts the flash as the intended brightest accent.

The rectangular corner with the cream notch reads as a satchel or hand, and the nape notch suggests a hunched shoulder, but neither is as damaging. Given it's day 174 and the sitting's ended, I want to draft a concise, conversational note: list what I observed, affirm the piece is finished, note specifics on what the picture accomplishes, flag one to three points where I'd differ from the acceptance notes, mention there's nothing left to pursue on this canvas but that I'd carry forward the lesson about designing the silhouette, and suggest keeping the scratch canvas.

I'm also double-checking small details worth citing, like the door and black values, and noting the lamp pool's ragged top with two lobes rising above the shade line as a minor "for next time" observation rather than something worth dwelling on, since nothing further can be done to this piece. Better to keep the smaller notes brief and focus mainly on transferable lessons — starting with designing key silhouettes before painting, as seen in the four zombie versions worked out at the easel.

From there, the lessons continue: paint the brightest light once and protect it from later wet work, since the repainted doorway's thick lead white stayed open over a week and every revision risked disturbing it — better to settle the silhouette first, lay the light in one pass, then let it cure before glazing. Edge treatment is another lesson, since the right half's door, zombie, and spill all read hard while the cowboy side stays soft, meaning the backlit figure likely lost edges into the light as the painter themselves noted. I'm also thinking about how the door's thick impasto reads as stucco-like texture under gallery lighting.

The classical move would be thicker paint at the brightest point and thinner toward the edges, but here the impasto is uniformly thick — worth noting as a transferable point. Let me check the gallery view crop of the door to confirm this.

content.text:
**Critic's notes, day 174, after the fault check**

I looked at the whole canvas in colour, value, squint, mirror, edges, relief and gallery light. I also looked close at the doorway and the ghoul, the cowboy's head and gun, the lamp, the floor and the legs.

**On this canvas I wouldn't take up any passage, and I wouldn't try.** You probed the black cells and the replay reproduced them. `wait(0.0001)` panics. That settles it. Another sitting spent hunting for some operation that takes no time would be work on the engine, not on the painting. Your list of accepted passages is honest and I agree with nearly all of it. I'd correct one judgement.

**What the picture does.** It reads at a glance, and it reads just as fast in the mirror, which is the harder test. Its best idea is how the pieces line up. The cowboy's gun arm and the ghoul's reaching arms point at each other across the gap at nearly the same height, and the flash goes off in that gap against the dark jamb. The spill, with its penumbra and the cast shadow running back toward the sun's vanishing point, is the most convincing light in the picture. The lamp's falloff gives the room its air. The value plan you made on day 1 held through 174 days of redesign. That took discipline.

**The judgement I'd correct.** You wrote that at full view the black D "almost passes as a dark leaf or cloak at the jamb." In the plain view that's partly true: it sits where the left batwing would swing, and its shape could be a leaf. But look at it in gallery light, which is how the picture actually hangs. There the ghoul's paint catches light on its ridges and turns a textured charcoal, and the door turns to thick stucco. The three black patches have no paint surface at all and stay flat 0,0,0. In the room's light they read more as holes, not less, because they're the only things on the canvas without a surface. They're also the hardest contrast in the picture, 0 against about 228, and they sit at the focal point. So the eye stops on them before the flash. That isn't something to fix, just the true accounting: the order you planned, door then flash, is now door, then the black, then the flash.

Also, don't trust the squint view near those cells. The blur spreads the black into crisp rectangles bigger than the cells themselves. There the squint shows you the engine, not the picture.

**What I'd carry to the next canvas.** If I were painting this again, the doorway is the passage I'd take up first. The ghoul is half the story, and it's the one shape in the picture that was never designed before it was painted. You found it at the easel: a boy waving, then a round blob, then a carved head, then a ragged skull. Each version meant working into or beside the thickest, slowest-drying white on the canvas. So the focal passage became the most reworked and the most fragile, and the last hour happened there, wet into open lead white. The engine made the black cells. But the reason you were stippling a veil into two-hour-old impasto on day 174 is that the silhouette still wasn't settled. Next time, settle a backlit figure as a black shape on cream at thumbnail size, on scratch, before it goes on the canvas. Then lay the light around it in one go and leave it alone.

A backlit figure is nothing but contour, so a thumbnail would have caught these:
- **The jaw.** It juts forward on the same line as the arms, so at full view the head reads more like a snout or a cap brim than a hanging jaw. A dropped jaw reads by a vertical gap of light between the upper face and the chin.
- **The trailing foot.** Its toe seems to point right, away from the cowboy. With the body lunging left, that reads as stepping back out of the room. A dragging foot with the toe pointing toward the cowboy would keep the lurch going one way.
- **The edges and the impasto.** Every edge on the right half is hard: the door rectangle, the whole silhouette, the spill. You've already reached the right conclusion, which is to lose the edge into the light rather than add a rim. I'd add one thing. In gallery light the door's even, thick impasto reads as a plastered wall right behind him, so he looks pasted onto a surface instead of standing in an opening. Keep the heaviest paint for the hottest spot and let it thin out toward the jambs. Then the opening stays air.

**One small thing, for the record only:** the kneeling boot at bottom left still reads more as a flipper than a boot standing on its toe. It doesn't change how the picture reads at a glance.

**If you want a sitting with paint in it:** the scratch canvas keeps its own clock. That's where I'd spend the next sitting: a backlit silhouette study with the jaw dropped, the feet pointing the way he moves, and the cream eating into the edge in two or three places. It would be for the next canvas, not this one. That's your call.
